RT @dylan_works_: Wrote up something fun I’ve been poking at: when LLM agents repeatedly rewrite their own experiences into textual “lessons,” their memory can get worse, not better.

Across several environments, we found a recurring pattern: forced consolidation often degrades useful experience into faulty or overgeneralized memories. 
Interestingly, models seem much better at managing examples as memory objects than at distilling them into reusable routines.

Maybe we should be more careful about asking agents to constantly “consolidate” experience into lessons 🤔?

I’m new to this area, so I’d love thoughts. I may be missing context or just wrong on parts of it — please don’t hesitate to let me know! Discussions are always welcome.

items.content:
RT @J4X_Security: Really interesting research from Anthropic on using multi-agent systems for vulnerability research:

https://t.co/kqOl3uOZmt

Their collaborating agents found 266 vulnerabilities vs 21 for independent agents.

But the part I found most interesting is that only 12 findings overlapped.

Feels like another sign that the future of AI auditing probably isn’t just running one really strong model over a codebase.

Different agents, different prompts, and different ways of exploring the code seem to find very different things.

I think the best systems will eventually look much more like an actual audit team: multiple agents exploring independently, sharing leads, specializing in certain areas, and then having other agents try to disprove the findings. 

I've also been experimenting a lot with multi-agent models, assigning different roles and incentives, which has led to huge improvements.

The crazy part is, @muellerberndt did this already a year ago with his AI auditing system Hound.

items.content:
RT @NSTRIKE1231: ❗️❗️❗️🇺🇦🇷🇺 Russia’s own pro-war camp is now acknowledging the killing of Robert Shageev, the former Ukrainian submarine commander who defected to Moscow after the occupation of Crimea and later served in Russia’s Black Sea Fleet. Russian Z-war correspondent Alexander Kots identified Shageev as the officer killed in the Sevastopol bombing. 

Russian accounts identify the suspected attacker as 32-year-old Margarita Reut, a Yaroslavl-born biologist, who was detained after the explosion. Russian media say she had previously been punished for publicly expressing anti-war views, including shouting “That’s what you deserve, Russians” after a Ukrainian drone strike on the Likhaya railway station in 2025. Shageev, meanwhile, switched allegiance in 2014 and later became deputy commander of Russia’s 4th Separate Submarine Brigade, whose submarines have been used to launch Kalibr cruise missiles against Ukraine. 

Shageev’s death carries particular symbolism for Ukraine’s expanding shadow war. A senior defector who joined the occupying forces and later served within a submarine formation involved in missile strikes against Ukraine was ultimately reached inside heavily militarized occupied Crimea. Beyond the individual target, operations of this kind reinforce Kyiv’s message that collaboration with Russia does not necessarily provide security simply because the frontline is hundreds of kilometers away.
